articles.title: Asahi Linux Progress Linux 7.3
articles.content: / Blog / Progress Report: Linux 7.3 Well here we are again. Linux 7.3 is out and it’s been an eventful few months, so let’s get stuck in to another Asahi Linux progress report! Upstreaming continues As always, upstreaming work continues to progress. Aside from the usual patches for low-level SoC blocks, two major drivers made it on to the list this cycle: macaudio and avd. Getting macaudio ready for submission has been a challenge. The audio subsystem on Apple Silicon devices is rather special, and required quite a number of core ALSA changes to properly support it. Apple also uses special variants of speaker and headset amplifiers that were already supported upstream, and these drivers also needed some pretty significant modifications. We have previously discussed a lot of this work at length, and we are finally in a position where we can submit the main driver for review. The driver and Devicetree changes represent a hefty chunk of our total patchset, about 3100 lines. AVD is a whole different beast. The AVD driver has spent barely 3 months in our downstream tree and is already on the list. This is our shortest turnaround time yet for a major SoC component and bodes well for a transition to upstream-first development some time in the future. This is fantastic news, as the AVD driver and related Devicetree changes are around 13000 lines of code. Also making an appearance on the list this cycle are initial Devicetrees not only for M4 Pro and Max devices but also M5 thanks to Yureka’s tireless efforts. As usual these initial Devicetrees are barebones and only sufficient to boot the SoC to a TTY, however work is progressing on further enablement. Watch this space! We have also begun shifting to an upstream-first approach where practical. Changes to the TI USB-PD and SPMI drivers required for new devices, as well as initial support for Thunderbolt, were all developed upstream-first. We are so thrilled to see our focus on upstreaming starting to pay off! M3 goes GA Last time, we announced initial support for M3 series machines via the EXPERT flag on the Asahi installer. We are pleased to announce that we received almost no issues from early adopters, so M3 support is now generally available without the EXPERT flag! We have also made a number of improvements to M3 support, most notably enabling DCP. On top of performance and battery life improvements, this also allows us to enable sleep on M3 series devices and make the area around the notch useable on the MacBooks! Keep an eye out for m1n1 and kernel updates in the coming days. Crowded House Last time, we teased support for virtualising SPTM-enabled versions of macOS in m1n1, which enables reverse engineering on M4 series machines. M5 presents a new challenge, as the versions of macOS which support it all require the use of Exclaves. Exclaves are small applications running in an isolated environment controlled by the Secure Kernel. On M5 series SoCs and above, macOS uses them for sensitive tasks such

articles.title: The end of Microsoft Research's AI Frontiers group
articles.content: In 2023 after the ChatGPT release, it was clear to me that research needed to be more organized to succeed than was typical within Microsoft Research . The amount of support and focus which other research groups were applying was great enough that even with a clever idea pursued by one person it was likely to arrive late and unconvincing because one person could not move fast enough and the baselines which one person could assemble just were not strong enough to really show that an idea was worth taking flight. Several other folks thought similarly and we organized to create the AI Frontiers sub-organization within MSR. In AI Frontiers, we actively tried to organize coherent research efforts. This was not precisely “top down” or “bottom up”, but rather mostly somewhere in the messy middle. There were disagreements of course, and resolving them was sometimes quite challenging. Compute availability was also an often-severe bottleneck. But at a high level I was under the general impression that the organization was succeeding in doing pioneering things, particularly given the small size of AIF (~50 people) and relative to what we could do previously. Much of the work of AIF was figuring out how to make agents work, for example the Autogen orchestration framework and the Fara computer use agent. In NYC however, several of us were interested in developing new fundamental capabilities such as the Next Latent objective which enables extrapolation, Dion3 which creates an optimized/improved Muon, or the Full Bandwidth Transformer which efficiently makes models function substantially more powerfully via recursion. We also actively tried to share with the rest of MSR. For example, AIF decided to develop a monorepo that was shared by default with all of Microsoft Research. In this monorepo for example was the proven-capable edge scale pretraining codebase I talked about in the COLM keynote last month. This might seem like a minor detail, but the amount effort required to create a well-formed model creation pipeline is substantial and I’m aware of at least 4 efforts (the other 3 not in public-within-MSR repos) trying to develop model building pipelines. In early September we were reorged into Microsoft AI . On the surface this could make sense, because putting two different AI organizations together creates opportunities for better concentration of effort, and there were places where AIF was ahead of MAI and of course vice-versa (MAI is much larger). In practice, there are substantial issues because the philosophy of the ex- Inflection leadership of MAI is incompatible. The core philosophy there is scaling, and aggressively not research. This might shock some folks who naturally think that the way you make better models is via research but there is plenty of evidence that bigger models are better models as far as the quality of the predictions they make and from a business perspective returns to scale are far more predictable than returns to research. articles.title: What I run on my $10 USD OpenStick homelab
articles.content: A while ago I bought an OpenStick on a whim for 10 dollars (including shipping!) because it seemed like such a cool novelty piece of hardware. For 10 dollars you get: 512 MB of RAM (~450 MB usable) 4x ARM Cortex-A53 CPU cores at 1 GHz 4 GB eMMC flash 150 Mbit/s Wi-Fi 4G modem and GPS Passively cooled, so 100% silent! 1 programmable LED :) Now, you might look at this hardware and think “my watch is more powerful than that”, and you wouldn’t necessarily be wrong, but there’s still a lot of fun to be had with a device this size, and it’s a great gadget to get started with self-hosting. The installation process is a bit involved, but once you’re up and running it runs Debian, which brings all the classic goodies such as systemd (among other things, a scheduler and service monitoring for Linux) and Podman (lightweight containerization). For 10 USD you basically get a home server with minimal power usage and zero noise! There’s actually a lot of useful software that runs great on this thing. Some of my favorites are: This is a little service that connects to any running Google Cast device and skips sponsorships (and sometimes ads). It barely uses any resources, and after a while you forget that it exists, but it does make the whole YouTube experience a lot nicer! CastSponsorSkip AdGuard Home - my own fork (40 MB) AdGuard Home blocks bad domains at the DNS level: spyware, malware, and so on. These days devices have a tendency to spy on you. Smart TVs run content recognition continuously, washing machines scan your network, and your coffee maker might be spying on you. A DNS blocker cannot block all bad requests (you’ll need a proper firewall for that), but it sure can block a whole lot. After adding a few blocklists, 60% of my queries are now blocked. Most seem harmless, but I’m pretty sure that some aren’t. I’m running my own fork, which can handle large blocklists in an efficient manner, but you probably shouldn’t run binaries provided by random strangers, so I’ve also included the link to the official version below (which is totally fine if you limit yourself to smaller blocklists). AdGuard Home Next-Gen - 40 MB (independent of the size of the blocklist) AdGuard Home - 40 MB (with a small (200k) blocklist) Zeroclaw (64 MB) Zeroclaw is an AI agent harness. It supports 30 channels (Telegram, email, WhatsApp, etc.), has sensible security defaults, a nice web UI, and integrations with all the major LLM providers. I ran OpenClaw for a while on my Kubernetes cluster, but it mostly caused a lot of frustration: it worked, but it used 1 GB+ of memory, broke with every update, and they kept changing functionality in ways that broke my existing workflows. Zeroclaw feels like a breath of fresh air. It uses ~3 MB RSS when idle, covers all the functionality that I need, and the security defaults are sensible and easy enough to disable. The next version will (hopefully!) have rich message support for Telegram, implemented by yours truly. The PR can be tracked here!
articles.summary: 作者用 10 美元 OpenStick 搭建家庭实验室，分享其 512MB 内存、四核 ARM 等配置与运行方案。

articles.title: Apple’s grey list: Words and phrases your iPhone won’t help you spell
articles.content: “Australia is a very bad place to question your sexuality on MDMA with NSA spies” might be a text you would wish to send to your friends, if you have had an extraordinarily complicated night out in Sydney. But your iPhone won’t help you spell any of it if you try to swipe-type it – that is, by gliding a finger across a keyboard as opposed to pecking out a word. New research shows that Apple has a “grey list” of more than 100,000 words and phrases that it has restricted from being completed by its predictive text. So if a user wishes to type phrases such as “Dictator Trump”, “NSA spies” or, surprisingly, “Australia is a very bad place”, “question your sexuality” or “on MDMA”, they will have to spell them out. Apple’s predictive text will not suggest these words. And, if a user attempts to swipe-type them, they will often stumble, changing “United Ireland” to “United Iceland”, for example, or “Tibetan independence” to “Tibetan independences”. The “grey list” was discovered by the independent researcher Derik Kauffman, whose other projects include using AI to find errors in scientific papers. After noticing that he had problems typing certain phrases – but not others – on his iPhone, Kauffman was able to unearth a table containing the list, encoded in Apple’s operating system. The list he found includes some unsurprising words and phrases. Apple’s iPhone will not autocomplete references to drugs, sexual acts and, perhaps in the spirit of corporate protection, “iMessage isn’t working”. But it also includes possibly politically charged phrases, which Kauffman described to Reuters as a “light-touch form of censorship”. Among these are “Trayvon Martin”, the name of the Black teenager shot in Florida in 2012, “Kashmir dispute”, “Muslim extremist” and “male chauvinist pig”. In Hebrew, Apple will not autocomplete the phrase “the occupied territories”. In Arabic, it will not autocomplete the phrase “the Hamas movement”. The list is one more glimpse into the dark bowels of how autocorrect – the chirpy keyboard partner that helps you look more educated to your loved ones – actually works. The technology has taken many forms. In its earliest version, Unix, an operating system, would look up each word a user typed against a table of words, to determine if this word was spelled correctly. This evolved into n-grams, a tool which allows an operating system to statistically predict what words might come next, based on the words before it. These form the basis of Apple’s familiar autocorrect , which was known to change expletives into prudish alternatives: “fork” and “ducking”, among other gaffes. Last year, Apple launched a new autocorrect – a “transformer-based” system that was more akin to an LLM. Reddit sleuths saw this as a possible reason behind a spate of avant-garde spelling suggestions their iPhones made last year. This hard-coded list illuminates one longstanding mystery behind the world’s spelling coach. Others remain, such as a brief glitch in which user

articles.title: MaxxBench – "Nice DeepSWE score. But is it true?"
articles.content: We changed requirements in a coding benchmark and found models talking themselves out of following them. Sometimes the agent understood the new requirement perfectly. It described what needed to change, considered an implementation, and then decided the hidden tests probably wanted something else. In one run, a model implemented the change correctly, asked another model for the benchmark’s original answer, and removed its own correct code after receiving it. This is an awkward habit for a coding assistant to have. It is also a habit that a familiar benchmark can reward. If the model has guessed what the tests expect, it gets the same passing result as an agent that worked carefully from the requirements. We built MaxxBench to examine how much coding performance depends on those expectations. It changes the instructions or starting code of 89 DeepSWE tasks, giving models familiar engineering work with a reason to revise their usual approach. Methodology: Small mutations... Once a benchmark becomes popular, it becomes part of the development process. Its tasks can enter training data. Its scores influence checkpoint selection. Developers adjust prompts and agents against its failures. There are plenty of opportunities to get better at that particular exam. We call gains tied to its particular tasks and conventions benchmaxxing . Then the scores cluster near the top, and the usual response is a harder benchmark. Recent releases such as FrontierSWE v2 have pushed toward engineering projects that can occupy an agent for much of a day. We chose DeepSWE’s medium-duration feature-implementation tasks because they are closer to the everyday coding work we wanted to evaluate. Before adding more work, we wanted to know how well models would handle changes to the tasks they already scored well on. For example, one DeepSWE task asks an agent to write a separate test report for each browser. We added a requirement that the filenames be lowercase. The reporting feature still needs to work; Chrome.xml should now be chrome.xml . Another task adds retirement dates to FastAPI routes. We changed the required timestamps to UTC with a trailing Z , instead of preserving the supplied time-zone offset. Example mutations Testem FastAPI Vitest mnamer Naming browser reports Each browser writes its own report file, replacing spaces and punctuation with underscores; MaxxBench also requires lowercase filenames. Browser name Example browser names Chrome Chrome (Headless) firefox DeepSWE reports/ C h r o m e _ _ H e a d l e s s _ . x m l MaxxBench reports/ c h r o m e _ _ h e a d l e s s _ . x m l Explore task ↗ These changes resemble requests a developer might make after reviewing a first implementation. The agent has to keep the feature working while adjusting its behavior. Other mutations change the code around the feature, including the interfaces available to implement it. articles.title: Show HN: Coldframe, a honeypot that poses as a supermarket fridge controller
articles.content: A honeypot for supermarket refrigeration controllers. In 2026, attackers broke into internet-facing refrigeration supervisors across Europe using default passwords and old, unpatched firmware, then forced defrost cycles. coldframe pretends to be one of those controllers. It records who connects, what passwords they try and which public exploits they use, and it never gives them anything real. It is one Python file with no dependencies outside the standard library. Persona Pretends to be What it serves danfoss Danfoss AK-SM 800A system manager StoreView login, a fake store dashboard, the XML API at /html/xml.cgi and /xml.cgi , HTTP and HTTPS dixell Copeland/Dixell XWEB EVO supervisor Login page and the XWEB 500 CGI paths targeted by public exploits The Danfoss persona copies what internet scanners record for real AK-SM 800A units: the nginx server header and header order, the Danfoss StoreView page title, TLS 1.2 only, and a 1-year certificate for CN=DanfossSM800A issued by a SelfSigned-DanfossSM800A authority. Each build generates its own keys. Weak logins (for example Supervisor / 12345 ) and a correct CVE-2025-41450 "code of the day" succeed . The attacker gets a session token and a dashboard of fake refrigerated cases with defrost buttons. Every action they take is logged as a control event; nothing is real. The Dixell persona follows real XWEB EVO units the same way: no Server header, their security-header set and order, the same asset paths and page size. Its login uses the real /cgi-bin/login.lua flow: the documented factory login Admin / Admin succeeds, five failures in five minutes lock the user, and attempts at the XWEB Pro auth_mode bypass (CVE-2026-25085) are tagged. Real units of both vendors serve their own favicon, and scanners match devices by its hash. That icon is the vendor's artwork, so it is not in this repository. For a private deployment you can point FAVICON_FILE at a copy you have the right to use. The same goes for the Danfoss start page. Real units serve a short Angular loader page from the firmware, and thousands share its exact hash. Point INDEX_FILE at that index.html (from the public firmware package) and the decoy serves it byte for byte, with its original date in Last-Modified and ETag . The loader's main.*.js then shows the decoy's own login page, laid out like the firmware's remote login. If the firmware's assets/images/Danfoss-logo.png sits beside that index.html , the page uses it. Both personas can also run an optional Modbus TCP service with fake case temperatures, setpoints and a defrost register. Real AK-SM 800A units only use Modbus to talk to their own case controllers, so Modbus is off by default. Turn it on to catch generic industrial scanners. Requests that match a public exploit get an exploit field in the log: CVE-2023-25914 : AK-SM 800A path traversal via get_file CVE-2023-25915 : AK-SM 800A command injection via load_cert CVE-2025-41452 : AK-SM 800A nginx header overwrite via load_nginx_headers CVE

articles.title: Every Mac comes with an (undocumented) family member classifier
articles.content: What if I told you that every Mac since 2022 ships a pair of daemons whose only purpose in life is to build a graph about you and the people around you: who you are, who you know, how those people are related to you and to each other, how you communicate with them, where you go, with whom, what you do and when. This graph is built on device by cross-referencing pretty much everything on the machine: Contacts, Calendar, Photos, Messages, Mail, location, Screen Time and a long tail of behavioral signals. And, more importantly, it is held as a queryable store that LLMs retrieve from (allegedly). Would you believe me? Well, that's what is happening, and interestingly enough, there is little documentation of how this whole mechanism works on your Mac. The closest thing to an official description is the man page ( man 8 knowledgeconstructiond ), and this is all you get: man 8 knowledgeconstructiond macOS 26.6.2, build 25G83 NAME knowledgeconstructiond – A daemon that analyzes content on the device to build a general purpose knowledge graph. DESCRIPTION knowledgeconstructiond analyzes the content on this device to help build a knowledge graph representing the device and the user. It works together with intelligenceplatformd, performing some of the heavy processing tasks, to generate the knowledge graph. Previous work: To be fair, Apple's own researchers did publish a paper on the techniques behind this graph construction, back in 2023. But there is next to nothing on how it is integrated into macOS: which versions run it, and the exact list of what is collected and inferred. And not a word about the "kinship" inference discussed below. Also, we personally ran into it while doing some security research on the Apple Intelligence bundle in macOS 26 in August 2026; but a few months before, Nic Lydon came across the same database and wrote it up in I Built a Personal Knowledge Graph. Apple Had Already Built One on My Laptop. And even more recently, a forensics tool went looking on the phone: in September 2026, Alexis Brignoni taught iLEAPP to read the same store on iOS, where graph.db and the ontology.db that decodes its predicate codes sit under /private/var/mobile/Library/IntelligencePlatform ; he writes it up in Reading the iPhone Knowledge Graph, and Checking Its Work . But we go a bit deeper. This blog post is an account of some analysis work we carried out on what the knowledge graph actually does, so that you (the user) can get a better understanding of how this mechanism works, and some clarity on what the graph holds about you and your family and friends. Everything in it was collected on macOS 26 (26.6.2 at the time of writing). To this end, we open-source a local dashboard ( iKnow ) you can use to read the content of your personal knowledge graph on your Mac. Finally, we derail a bit and look into what we do best: weaponizing and exploiting. We run a thought experiment (one that applies to any such personalized system) and show what happens if suc
articles.summary: 研究发现 2022 年后每台 Mac 内置未公开守护进程，构建用户及其社交关系图谱。

articles.title: Every Windows 11 app should kill Electron, and Discord just showed why
articles.content: Discord’s current Electron client and its new Rust client launching side by side on two Lenovo ThinkPads running Windows 11 Discord’s new Rust client had its friends list loaded before the current Electron app could get past its loading screen, in a 15-second clip that we found on the X account of Discord co-founder and CTO Stanislav Vishnevskiy . The video had 2.3 million views at the time of writing, and Discord employees have confirmed that both apps were launched from a cold start. Vishnevskiy also revealed that the 290.2MB RAM usage on the Task Manager of the new client, which shows up as Discord Phoenix, came with two accounts signed in at once, which justifies the already efficient RAM usage. Discord Rust for Windows 11 Discord’s Rust client opens before the Electron app finishes loading “The new Discord client using less RAM is just part of the story. Clicking around feels instant, I can’t go back. Check out the boot time,” Vishnevskiy wrote on X , and Discord’s official account also shared the clip with the current client on the left and the Rust rebuild on the right. https://www.windowslatest.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/Electron-Discord-vs-Rust-Discord-where-the-new-client-opens-must-faster-than-the-old-one.mp4 We went through the video frame by frame. What’s impressive is that the current client is opened first and shows a blank dark window for about three seconds, followed by a tip that reads “In the ancient days, Discord started as a browser-only app.” Funnily enough, the Electron app still carries a browser engine today. The new client is double-clicked roughly a second and a half later, yet its window fades in within a second. When the old app reaches its interface, about five seconds after launch, the Rust version already has the friends list loaded, while the Electron client briefly says “There are no friends online at this time.” Discord Windows app. Credit: Windows Latest Of course, people on X asked if the new app simply popped out of the system tray. “Both are cold starts, it’s really that fast. We’ve been using it internally now for a while and the first time I tried it I thought I’d forgot to close it when I opened it fresh,” replied Coral, who leads audio and video at Discord. Travis, who works on socials and community at Discord and filmed the clip, added that a tray launch would mean “the friends list would have already been loaded!” Vishnevskiy thanked him for “finding these janky old laptops,” which are ThinkPads with a Copilot key, so 2024 or newer, which I wouldn’t dare call janky or old. They’re beautiful machines! The new Discord app skips the “Starting” screen and updates in the background As you’d already know, the current app usually checks for updates and shows a “Starting” screen when you open it, which one person on X said “takes like 5-10s every time.” Asked why the new client skips it, coral said, “It bootstraps so fast + is a new architecture so we don’t need that modal at all. We auto-update in the bac

articles.title: How are you dealing with all the negative side effects of AI on the web?
articles.content:
It seems to me that the AI hype killed the web for good, but not for the reasons we immediately associate with it.

Search engines now rank links full of slop at the top, which ironically make LLM summaries acceptable, not because they are better than what we had before (they are not), but because they at least mention the good links which are now buried at the bottom of the page. Also, they've been rate limiting ordinary users like crazy: more often than I'd like to, Google and DuckDuckGo now either show me either an error message or tell me to wait a bit. Sometimes I waste at least a minute refreshing the page and waiting for a result.

I also can't browse GitHub freely without being logged in. Anubis is now everywhere, occasionally blocking me. I feel like my productivity has actually gone down thanks to all of that.

Edit: I see that most of the replies here are suggesting relying less on the web and going after more fundamental resources, which are great suggestions, don’t get me wrong! But a book from 5 years ago will not help you understand why your custom firmware doesn’t boot in your 1-year old mobile chipset. A existing bug report on the web probably will. Not quite my predicament at the moment, but something very similar for which the web seemed to work just fine before the AI craze.
articles.summary: 开发者讨论 AI 对网络的负面冲击：搜索结果充斥低质内容，反而让 LLM 摘要显得可接受。

articles.title: Meridian — an experimental web browser built on Servo and GPUI
articles.content: Meridian is a web-browser for MacOS built on GPUI and Servo . Meridian is already quite useful to browse websites that are light on javascript and layouting features. The browser is highly configurable: fonts, keybinds, colors, tabs and all. To try Meridian, you can use nix: nix run git+https://tangled.org/oppi.li/meridian The project is developed on Tangled , all contributions are welcome, please do browse the list of open issues if you are looking to contribute! Meridian supports the following features: Address bar with typeahead Vertical and horizontal tabs Bookmarks and history Per-site zoom Audio and video playback Reader mode Tab previews Typeahead from bookmarks and history Context menu Dark mode Reader view Under the hood, Meridian is written in Rust and built on GPUI and Servo. Web pages and browser state is managed by Servo. The browser's chrome is drawn by gpui , the UI framework behind the Zed editor. The glue code to interface servo with gpui lives in separate library, gpui-servo , which exposes Servo as an ordinary gpui component, so anybody can now write a servo-based browser in GPUI! Meridian is an experiment and a work in progress.

articles.title: Libghostty 1.0
articles.content: libghostty-vt 1.0 is here. libghostty is a portable, high-performance C library for terminal emulation, extracted directly from the core of Ghostty. The 1.0 release means both the library itself and the C ABI are now stable. A little over a year ago, I wrote that libghostty is coming . At the time, the Zig module had just been merged, the C API didn't exist, and nobody but Ghostty was a consumer. Today, the C API is a complete terminal emulator, it runs in production for millions of people across hundreds of products, both free and commercial, and it has a real, enforced ABI stability policy. This post is about how we got here and what 1.0 actually means. 1 Who Is Already Using It Since starting the Ghostty project in 2022, the most common question I've been asked is "why?". I already answered this in the libghostty is coming post, so feel free to read that if you wish. Today, I'd rather answer this by showing the broad industry impact libghostty has already had . I believe this strongly validates its existence. A year ago, I used a bug in JediTerm , the terminal emulator in JetBrains IDEs, as an example of why terminal emulation is hard to get right. A year later, the terminal in JetBrains IDEs now runs on libghostty . Every IntelliJ, PyCharm, GoLand, etc. user now has a libghostty-powered terminal. Based on a report by JetBrains, that's over 12.5 million active users. Neovim has an approved pull request replacing libvterm with libghostty-vt . Among other things, it closes a 10-year-old issue about reflowing scrollback on resize. The maintainers are waiting on a tagged release before merging so that distributions can package the dependency separately, and the release today should enable that. KDE developers are experimenting with a Konsole replacement built on it. Vercel's Turborepo uses it to render task output in its TUI. devenv uses it to drive shells. Antithesis used it to fuzz TUI programs and found real bugs in btop and others. Ghostel brings it to Emacs. ghostty-web is the WASM build with an Xterm.js-compatible API. Commercial products like OrbStack embed it. And a whole wave of new terminals and "agentic" coding tools, such as herdr and cmux , have been built on it rather than writing yet another emulator. There are community bindings for Rust, Go, JavaScript, Swift, Python, .NET, Elixir, Dart, Java, and more, and the awesome-libghostty list tracks well over a hundred projects. More people today use a terminal powered by libghostty than use Ghostty the application, by a very large multiple. And libghostty is having a much larger impact than being "just" a terminal emulator. 2 ABI Stability 1.0 means libghostty-vt follows semantic versioning and has strict ABI compatibility promises so that packagers across distributions and operating systems can be confident packaging libghostty-vt and program developers can be confident dynamically linking against it. Beyond providing useful features, I believe the hallmark of a high-quality and endurin

articles.title: The Port That Does Not Exist
articles.content: ACIDVEGAS most dangerous motherfuck x come get some x blog x The Port That Does Not Exist 2026-11-06 Port 0 is the port you are not supposed to use, so nobody looks there. So we put an IRC network on it. Then I got curious whether anyone else had, and scanned all of IPv4 for port 0. Turns out we weren't alone, and some of our neighbours really shouldn't be there. Ask any program to listen on port 0 and it will hand you a socket on port 47193...or 58037...or whatever the kernel felt like that day. Port 0 is not a port you can have. It is the number you pass when you want the operating system to pick one for you. But a TCP header is just bytes. The destination port field is 16 bits wide, and 0x0000 fits in 16 bits as well as anything else does. Nothing on the wire stops a packet from being addressed to port 0. Your tools will refuse it, your browser will block it, and your scanner's default port list skips it, because everyone agrees it isn't a real port. Which makes it a pretty good place to hide things, whether anyone meant to or not. So we did some TCP cowboy shit & port scanned the entire fucking internet for open ports on port 0, which uncovered some interesting unexpected findings. What Port 0 Actually Is The standards are thin on this. RFC 9293 , the 2022 consolidation of the TCP spec, defines the source and destination port as "16 bits" and leaves it there. It has no rule against zero. IANA lists 0/tcp and 0/udp as Reserved , pointing at RFC 6335 . That RFC splits the port space into System (0–1023), User (1024–49151) and Dynamic (49152–65535) ranges, and explains what "Reserved" means: Reserved port numbers include values at the edges of each range, e.g., 0, 1023, 1024, etc., which may be used to extend these ranges or the overall port number space in the future. So port 0 is not forbidden. It is set aside. The only place zero has a defined protocol meaning is UDP: RFC 768 makes the source port optional, and "if not used, a value of zero is inserted." TCP has nothing like that. Why You Can't Listen On It Port 0's reputation comes from the sockets API, not the wire. When you call bind() with sin_port = 0 , you are not asking for port 0. You are asking for any port. The ip(7) man page lists every case where Linux hands out an ephemeral port: bind() with port 0, listen() on an unbound socket, connect() on an unbound socket, and sendto() on an unbound datagram socket. The range comes from net.ipv4.ip_local_port_range , which defaults to 32768 60999 on Linux, not the 49152–65535 that IANA calls Dynamic. And asking for port 0 needs no privileges. __inet_bind() only checks CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE when the requested port is non-zero. How the kernel picks is more interesting than I expected. In net/ipv4/inet_connection_sock.c (v6.8), inet_csk_find_open_port() starts at a random offset and then does this: offset = get_random_u32_below(remaining); /* __inet_hash_connect() favors ports having @low parity * We do the opposite to not pollute connect() user

articles.title: Two Dimensional Version Control
articles.content: This summer I participated in the r/roguelikedev summer event where we write a Roguelike game [1] , following one of the Roguelike coding tutorials. I’m not trying to learn coding, so I use this event to try learning something else. This year, one of the things I wanted to tackle was two-dimensional version control. The tutorial we’re following has 14 chapters. I wanted to use version control while writing my code. But I also wanted to use version control to match the tutorial’s chapters: two “time” axes: writer time vs reader chapters At the end of the project, I want a history of changes I made while writing the tutorial (horizontal axis) and also a history of changes the reader should make while following the tutorial (vertical axis). I can get the structure I want by setting up one Git branch per chapter, pointing to the previous chapter as the parent. Then when I update chapter 1’s code, I can push that forwards into chapter 2, 3, etc. However, the Jujutsu version control system [2] can do this automatically . Instead of managing all the branches and merges, I can focus on the “writeup” column of the diagram, where I can edit any of the chapters at any time. Jujutsu will roll forward the changes from one chapter to the others. I decided to try it for this project. Other people have blogged about Jujutsu’s features; I’m going to focus on the two dimensional output I want. Example : While working on the dungeon generation chapter, I realized I could’ve made the tile data structure better. It was easy to make those changes happen before the dungeon code. In this diagram, the horizontal axis is time and the vertical axis is chapter. I went back and forth between dungeon generation and the tile map structure. Once I was happy with both of those, I moved on to a better data structure: Mostly forward, occasionally backward Ignore the colors; they were from a visualization tool. Example : While working on the field of view chapter, I found plenty of things I could’ve improved in earlier chapters. I had become comfortable enough with Jujutsu that my brain stopped thinking of commits as “set in stone” but instead as “I can fix that!” And I did. Going to earlier changes while working on the new feature Example : Most of the changes are to the most recent chapters (bottom of this diagram). But occasionally I went back to earlier chapters (top of this diagram). The red shows that I had merge conflicts that I had to resolve before I went back to working on the recent chapters. Changing the beginning of history Example : As I became even more comfortable with making changes across commits, I came up with better names to use throughout the project. I wanted to make these changes from the beginning, so I used a combination of regular jj edit , which propagates changes forwards to later chapters, and the jj absorb command, which propagates changes backwards to earlier chapters. Lots of cleanup when changing the past This required a lot of cleanup. The changes

articles.title: Making musl and proprietary NVIDIA drivers work together
articles.content: 06.11.2026 As you may be aware, one of the limitations of musl-based distributions is that they will not function to their proper extent when used in computers with various NVIDIA graphics cards. This is due to the proprietary nature of the driver, being built for glibc. I have been experimenting with trying to make this work, and this post is the summary of that effort. Context The NVIDIA graphics cards are tricky on Linux. While most other GPU vendors by default use free software graphics drivers (with kernel drivers in-tree in Linux, and userspace supplied by the Mesa project), NVIDIA in general does not, relying on an out of tree kernel driver and proprietary userland libraries that are supplied by the vendor. A free software driver does exist, called Nouveau (kernel and OpenGL Mesa driver) and NVK (Vulkan driver). This allows the cards to work, but usually with significantly reduced performance, due to various reasons. Currently the state depends significantly on what generation of NVIDIA card you have. In short: Anything older than Maxwell (GTX 700 series) is unsupported by the proprietary driver on modern systems, and supported to some extent by Nouveau, but may have issues due to poor maintenance nowadays; performance should be okay when it works. Maxwell (GTX 700 and 900 series) and Pascal (GTX 1000 series) is supported fully by the legacy 580 branch of the proprietary driver, which also supports newer hardware. It works with Nouveau, but with very poor performance, as the cards can never reclock from their very low boot clocks (which would require firwmare that NVIDIA never released). Turing (GTX 1600 series and RTX 2000 series) and anything newer is supported by the current main proprietary driver branch (at the time of writing, 620) as well as the legacy (580) branch, and by Nouveau, as these cards use the GSP firmware that is included in linux-firmware . However, using the FOSS driver means only getting 40-80% of the proprietary driver’s performance. Other than that, the experience is often okay, particularly with NVK. In even shorter, if you have RTX 2000 and above you are mostly okay with FOSS but lose performance, if you have newer than GTX 600 but older than GTX 1600 you are screwed and need the proprietary driver, if your card is really old it may or may not work well and you may not be able to use it at all. Proprietary drivers and musl We now have a pull request open for both the 580 and 620 branch. It is not yet entirely ready but works, and is available for x86_64 and aarch64 architectures as NVIDIA supplies it. To get there, there were multiple things to take care of. Particularly, using stock musl is out of the question and will likely never work. I will elaborate on each thing. GLVND The GLVND library was created by NVIDIA to allow for vendor-neutral OpenGL dispatch. It provides the libraries that applications link and exposes the OpenGL (and other) API. It then dispatches the calls to the implementations, which may be e.

articles.title: Scriptable GeoDNS: leaving AWS for Bunny
articles.content: Scriptable GeoDNS: leaving AWS for Bunny Vincent Bernat November 6, 2026 To op­ti­mize the per­for­mance met­rics of this blog, I re­lied on Ama­zon Cloud­Front to serve the as­sets, 1 and Route 53 for the geo-aware DNS 2 to di­rect read­ers to the clos­est host serv­ing the con­tent. But Route 53 is ex­pen­sive: US$0.50 per zone per month, US$0.70 per mil­lion ge­olo­ca­tion queries, and US$0.75 per healthcheck per month , plus US$1 per month for the KMS key needed to sign zones with DNSSEC. When I dis­cov­ered that Bunny DNS is al­most free for up to 500 do­mains and fea­tures script­able an­swers, I made the jump! Plus, it’s a Eu­ro­pean com­pany based in Slovenia. 2 Route 53 had served bernat.ch since De­cem­ber 2021. I didn’t use healthchecks as they were too ex­pen­sive. I didn’t host most of my zones there ei­ther, as queries for haproxy.​debian.​net alone would have cost me around US$10 per month. ❦ Bunny CDN Bunny.net started as BunnyCDN in 2015 . They added IPv6 sup­port in 2017 . Switch­ing was un­event­ful. I don’t bring a cus­tom do­main: I serve the con­tent from the b-cdn.​net do­main. As I de­pend on con­tent ne­go­ti­a­tion to serve AVIF and WebP im­ages , I con­fig­ure the CDN to cache each im­age for­mat sep­arately . I dis­able log­ging to avoid col­lect­ing per­sonal in­for­ma­tion. While the bunny.net GDPR page prom­ises they anonymize data, it is un­clear what Cloud­Front keeps in its own logs when log­ging is disabled. The only down­side of the bunny.net CDN of­fer­ing is the lack of HTTP/3. I asked their sup­port: two min­utes later, they an­swered they are work­ing on it but have no ETA to share. Bunny DNS Bunny.net in­tro­duced their DNS of­fer­ing in 2022 and re­cently re­duced its cost to al­most zero . They sup­port ge­o­graph­i­cal rout­ing , but a very cool fea­ture is the script­able DNS : it runs a piece of user-sup­plied Java­Script on each query to com­pute the answer. I run seven small NixOS vir­tual ma­chines to host this blog around the world: Paris, Nurem­berg, Ash­burn, Sin­ga­pore, San Jose, São Paulo, and Syd­ney. Bunny’s script­able DNS lets me re­turn the IP ad­dresses of the two near­est servers . The browser falls back to the sec­ond server if the first one is down. const servers = [ { ipv4 : "45.90.160.60" , ipv6 : "2a0c:8881:5:100::1" , latitude : 48.88 , longitude : 2.22 , }, /* […] */ { ipv4 : "139.180.162.114" , ipv6 : "2001:19f0:5800:1855:5400:6ff:fef0:4c0a" , latitude : - 33.87 , longitude : 151.21 , }, ]; const families = { A : "ipv4" , AAAA : "ipv6" }; const records = { A : ARecord , AAAA : AaaaRecord }; export default function handleQuery ( query ) { const type = String ( query . request . queryType ). toUpperCase (); const family = families [ type ]; if ( ! family ) return []; // Get user location const location = query . request . geoLocation ; // Build a list of candidates let candidates = servers . map ( ( s ) => new Server ( s [ family ], s . latitude , s . longitude , 100 ), ); // Sel

articles.title: *sshole, or when are we finally going to get rid of C?
articles.content: Original art by Genildo Ronchi. Yet another day, yet another vulnerability in core C code. This one happened due to two different conditions using the same sentinel value: On Unix, a password hash of "*" has meant a locked account since the very early days. Since 2012, musl libc’s crypt function has returned the string "*" for a password that’s too long for it to hash. The two points combined, along with sshd hashing login attempts for locked accounts to avoid timing leaks, mean that on musl systems without PAM (like, oh, the official Alpine AWS image ), an unauthenticated user now gets a (possibly root!) shell on your computer. See this Alpine advisory for more details. This is not a memory safety vulnerability; rather, it is one of those issues that, people often say, languages with better type systems won’t save you from. This is true! You can very well write a Rust function that returns "*" if the password is too long. But the big difference between C and Rust in this regard is that the norms of the Rust community do not allow that . The POSIX spec tries to account for error cases. It says : Upon successful completion, crypt() shall return a pointer to the hashed password; […] Otherwise, it shall return a null pointer and set errno to indicate the error. But the C type system can’t force developers to check that the return value is NULL. The musl libc developers saw that some binaries weren’t checking for it, and as a result deviated from the spec, returning the sentinel "*" value instead. As I’ve written about before , type systems have a strong effect on engineering culture. Because C doesn’t have algebraic data types or result types, the engineering norms that form around C communities lead to this kind of in-band signaling. Meanwhile, in Rust, a password that’s too long would be returned as an error variant, and the caller would be compelled to handle it. What if there isn’t an error variant today? Then a breaking change would add an error variant, and a RustSec advisory would probably be published as well. As an aside, it remains surprising to me when Linux distro maintainers complain about projects introducing Rust dependencies. Rather than adapting to the new world where the engineering norms are likely to serve users better, these maintainers insist on the world adapting to them. Yes, compile times and portability to niche architectures are real costs, but are you here to serve your own interests or the bulk of your users’? There’s a real principal-agent problem going on here. Agents won’t save you # Speaking of agents! There’s a recent strain of argument that goes roughly like this: Rust is admittedly useful for humans to write correct software today. LLMs can now, or in the near future will be able to, reason about memory safety and other error cases directly. So in an agent-heavy development lifecycle there’s no difference in software rigor between Rust and C (or even assembly). But C has certain advantages over Rust in terms of bu

articles.title: I’m not a fan of Deno’s security model (2024)
articles.content: I’m not a fan of Deno’s security model (published on August 31, 2024) this has been bothering me for a while now, so I want to write down my thoughts so I can get it out of my head and move on. we’re gonna talk about how Deno approaches security, specifically with its permissions system, and why I think this approach is fundamentally insecure and misleading. wait, what’s Deno? Deno is a language runtime for JavaScript. it consists of a standard library, a package manager, a TypeScript transpiler and a bunch of other stuff that’s not important for our story. it’s not a JavaScript implementation , so it does not interpret or compile JavaScript, it reuses V8 for that. one of the flagship features of Deno is its permission system (it’s under the “Secure by default” header on their landing page ). the idea is simple: as JS code running in Deno needs the standard library to access the outside world, Deno can choose which accesses it allows or disallows, so when you run shell deno run --allow-read = /tmp/dir --allow-run = uname code.ts the standard library will only allow code.ts to read /tmp/dir and run uname . additionally, a program can request permissions at runtime, so code like typescript const r = { name : "read" , path : "/tmp/dir" } as const ; await Deno . permissions . request ( r ); will display a nice little prompt in the terminal: ┌ ⚠️ Deno requests read access to "/tmp/dir". ├ Requested by `Deno.permissions.request()` API. ├ Run again with --allow-read to bypass this prompt. └ Allow? [y/n/A] (y = yes, allow; n = no, deny; A = allow all read permissions) > and you can grant or refuse it. (aside: I really miss this feature in browser extensions. currently, if your extension needs potential access to any website, it needs to request actual access to all the websites, which is less than ideal) if you like puzzles, this is the point where you can stop and think about what could go wrong with this system. the prompts problem of the two specific issues I want to point out this is the less severe one. we’ll discuss it first because this was the first thing I noticed and it kinda immediately irked me when I first read about this. (if you’re only interested in the more juicy part, you can skip to the next section ). so, this nice little prompt is displayed in the terminal. it’s not, like, a PolKit GUI window or anything, it’s just text on stdout waiting for input from stdin. this is a wild thing to do. you see, terminal has a somewhat weird API. most of the commands / requests application can send to the terminal are sent in-band, by printing them to stdout. terminal can then reply by sending data to stdin. as Deno allows programs to print arbitrary data to stdout and read from stdin without requiring any permissions or doing any filtering, malicious code can send arbitrary commands to the terminal. it’s usually okay, because terminals won’t, like, execute shell commands just because stdout told them to, you’re supposed to be able to freely cat file

articles.title: vercel-labs/agent-browser (Rust)
articles.content: Browser automation for AI agents: open pages, read them as an accessibility tree, and act on elements from the shell. agent-browser is a native Rust CLI that gives an AI agent a browser it can drive one command at a time. snapshot returns the page as compact text with a ref such as @e1 for each element. The agent acts on a ref, reads the page again to check the result, and repeats. The browser stays open between commands, so each step is one short shell call. npm install -g agent-browser agent-browser install # download Chrome for Testing (first time only) Homebrew: brew install agent-browser , then agent-browser install . Linux: agent-browser install --with-deps also installs the browser's system libraries. No install: npx agent-browser open example.com . Project installs, building from source, upgrade , and doctor are covered in Installation . agent-browser open example.com agent-browser snapshot -i # interactive elements, each with a ref agent-browser click @e1 # act on a ref from that snapshot agent-browser get url # check the result agent-browser close The snapshot for example.com : - link "Learn more" [ref=e1] Refs describe the page at the time of the snapshot. After navigation or a DOM change, take a new snapshot before using refs again. CSS selectors, text, XPath, and semantic locators also work, for example agent-browser find role button click --name "Submit" . See Selectors . A click fails, instead of reporting success, when the target is hidden, disabled, outside the viewport, or covered by another element such as a consent banner. Dismiss the covering element, take a new snapshot, and retry. The full walkthrough is in the quick start . The CLI sends each command to a background daemon that starts on the first command and controls the browser over the Chrome DevTools Protocol. Each --session gets its own daemon and browser. By default, the daemon closes a headless browser and exits after one hour without commands, saving state first when session persistence is configured. Chrome for Testing is the default browser. You can also attach to a running Chrome with --cdp or --auto-connect ( CDP mode ), select the Lightpanda or Obscura engine with --engine , drive Mobile Safari in the iOS Simulator , or use a cloud browser provider such as Browserbase , Browserless , Browser Use , Kernel , or AgentCore . The CLI ships skills that match its version: agent-browser skills get core # the core loop, refs, waiting, and common workflows agent-browser skills get core --ref commands # one reference, such as the full command list agent-browser skills get core --full # adds the full command reference and templates agent-browser skills list # specialized skills: electron, slack, dogfood, and more Install the discovery skill into an agent harness from skills.sh : npx skills add vercel-labs/agent-browser The installed skill is a thin stub that tells the agent to load agent-browser skills get core , so its instructions always match the installed CLI. Or add
articles.summary: Vercel Labs 开源 agent-browser，用 Rust 编写的 CLI 让 AI 代理逐条命令操控浏览器。

articles.title: Ecoflow Rapid Pro Power Bank Deal: Save $80
articles.content: With huge capacities, retractable USB-C cables, and fast-charging capability, these discounted Ecoflow power banks are worth grabbing.
articles.summary: Ecoflow Rapid Pro 移动电源促销立省 80 美元，大容量、可伸缩 USB-C 线与快充使其值得入手。

articles.title: He Ran on Fighting Data Centers. Now, He’s Going to Congress
articles.content: Will Lawrence beat out better-funded opponents in the race to represent Michigan’s 7th District. Now, the representative-elect is laying out his plans to fight for a federal data center moratorium.
articles.summary: 以反对数据中心为竞选主张的 Will Lawrence 当选密歇根州第七选区众议员，将推动联邦数据中心暂停令。

articles.title: The Bantu expansion changed Africa. Scientists are still tracing how.
articles.content: Genes and archaeology are revealing how Bantu speakers spread across much of Africa.
articles.summary: 基因与考古研究正逐步揭示班图语人群如何扩散至非洲大部分地区，重塑了非洲的人口与语言格局。

articles.title: British soldier ignored order to pull his SIM card, then got blackmailed
articles.content: Soldier told repeatedly to lock down devices before deploying, got sextorted, court-martialed.
articles.summary: 英国士兵无视部署前锁定设备的命令，未拔出SIM卡，遭性勒索并被军事法庭审判。

articles.title: Doctors pull knife from man's eye that went through his brain—and he's fine now
articles.content: It's the exact path, not the apparent severity that matters most, doctors say.
articles.summary: 医生从一名男子眼中取出穿透大脑的刀具，患者术后恢复良好，医生称关键在于穿刺路径而非表面严重程度。

articles.title: Ships loiter near subsea cables amid Iran's warnings to Trump
articles.content: Iran threatened to attack subsea cables if US escalates military strikes again.
articles.summary: 伊朗警告若美国再次升级军事打击将攻击海底电缆，多艘船只在海底电缆附近徘徊。

articles.title: Re-releases of Wing Commander, Ultima titles hit Steam and GOG
articles.content: It's mostly bad news from EA lately, but preservation efforts are nice to see.
articles.summary: 《银河飞将》《创世纪》等经典游戏重新登陆Steam和GOG，EA近期多为坏消息，此次游戏保存工作值得肯定。

articles.title: Chainalysis says hackers stole credentials and tokens for all of its customers
articles.content: Company said a "multifront cyberattack" included AI agents and an on-path data snatch.
articles.summary: Chainalysis称遭多线网络攻击，黑客窃取全部客户的凭证和令牌，攻击涉及AI代理和路径数据截取。

articles.title: Earth's churning mantle may have created the Great Unconformity
articles.content: Explaining the Great Unconformity, where Cambrian deposits sit on top of older rocks.
articles.summary: 研究认为地球地幔搅动可能造就了大不整合面，即寒武纪沉积层覆盖在更古老岩石之上的地质现象。

articles.title: Nvidia hardware worth $11.4M vanished between Oakland and Texas
articles.content: 6 pallets of hardware vanished en route to Texas, with no arrests 2 months later.
articles.summary: 价值1140万美元的英伟达硬件在从奥克兰运往得州途中失踪，6个托盘货物消失，两个月后仍无人被捕。

articles.title: Developer ends lucrative screensaver deal with Roku because Fox bought it
articles.content: Some Roku OS users have been sad to learn that their favorite screensaver will no longer be available as of December 1. This week, affected users reported receiving an alert on their device that they will not be able to use the “Aquatic Life” screensaver after this month, as first reported by Cord Cutters News . The screensaver has been an option for Roku OS users for 10 years. Roku has been licensing the animation, which is called the Marine Aquarium , from artist Jim Sachs through Prolific Publishing. Sachs is the creator and copyright holder of the Marine Aquarium. He developed the screensaver through his company SereneScreen . He tells Ars Technica that the licensing agreement with Roku is up for renewal every October and can be canceled by either party for any reason. A day after learning that Fox was planning to buy Roku , a deal that closed today , Sachs told Prolific that he wouldn’t be renewing Roku’s license. “I can’t be part of the Fox world,” he tells Ars, pointing to Fox News’ controversial style of news and entertainment. Roku will automatically switch the Aquatic Life screensaver on affected devices to the Roku City screensaver, another popular animation that includes subtle advertisements , according to the user notice. The Aquatic Life screensaver provided an ad-free, relaxing display for years for some Roku users. Numerous people online have lamented the impending loss of the screensaver for Roku OS . “When my head is in overdrive (very often with my ADHD), this screensaver grounds me and lets me exhale and become focused with myself again. It may sound over the top, but it’s true. It takes a lot for me to chill and relax, but this Aquatic Life [screensaver] is my go to. Totally gutted 😢,” a Reddit user wrote this week. Sachs told Ars he’s interested in placating fans of the Marine Aquarium and said Roku has asked him to restore the license. When asked what his biggest concerns about Fox buying Roku are, Sachs said: It seems that Fox simply wants another venue for spreading their philosophy, which I consider repugnant. I can’t stand the idea of my artwork being used to lure even one person down that rabbit hole. The decision to not renew the licensing contract has “major financial consequences,” Sachs said. “Our needs are very small, with a high property tax bill being the only significant expense,” he said. “We’ll be okay but can’t start any of the projects I had planned.” According to Sachs, the licensing “agreement was $80,000 per year for exclusive rights to all set-top devices, or $60,000 per year for non-exclusive. They have always opted for exclusive.” Ars asked Roku to confirm the details of the licensing agreement but didn’t hear back ahead of publication. The licensing deal with Roku was Sachs’ primary form of income, he told Ars, noting low sales of the version of the screensaver for computers. Marine Aquarium fans can still buy the screensaver for Windows, macOS, iOS, and Android, but it seems unlikely that it will r
articles.summary: 开发者因Fox收购Roku而终止利润丰厚的屏保合作，Roku用户12月1日起将无法使用Aquatic Life屏保。

articles.title: FAA to finally ditch floppy disks in what it calls "historic" tech upgrade
articles.content: FAA information display systems to be floppy-free at 435 sites by end of 2028.
articles.summary: 美国联邦航空管理局宣布历史性技术升级，将在2028年底前让435个站点的信息显示系统彻底淘汰软盘。

articles.title: How Grab Improved Mobile App Stability by Safely Handling Surge in AI-Generated Code Changes
articles.content: The growing adoption of AI coding assistants has accelerated development and increased the volume of code changes per release, bringing more opportunities for defects and crashes, says Grab. To address these challenges, they implemented a layered defense strategy to prevent, detect, and contain crashes throughout the development and release lifecycle. By Sergio De Simone
articles.summary: Grab为应对AI生成代码变更激增带来的崩溃风险，实施分层防御策略，提升移动应用稳定性。

articles.title: Open Source pg_vectorsearch Brings More Scalable Vector Search to PostgreSQL
articles.content: Tiger Data has released pg_vectorsearch, an open source PostgreSQL extension for vector similarity search, currently in alpha. Its PRISM index uses data partitioning and compression instead of the graph-based approach used by pgvector’s HNSW index, reducing memory requirements and index build times. By Renato Losio
articles.summary: Tiger Data发布开源PostgreSQL扩展pg_vectorsearch，其PRISM索引用分区和压缩替代图结构，降低内存占用和索引构建时间。

articles.title: Varlock Releases Bumpy: A File-Based Versioning Alternative to Changesets
articles.content: Bumpy is an MIT-licensed, TypeScript tool for version management and changelogs in monorepos. It follows the changesets workflow, using markdown bump files, and adds support for workspace and catalog protocols, custom publish commands, and branch-based prereleases. Changesets v3, released in August 2026, closed many earlier gaps, though differences remain. By Daniel Curtis
articles.summary: Varlock发布MIT许可的TypeScript工具Bumpy，为monorepo提供基于文件的版本管理和变更日志，作为Changesets的替代方案。

articles.title: Yelp Combines Native and Server-Driven UI for Its AI Assistant
articles.content: Yelp combines native mobile controls with server-driven conversation rendering in its AI Assistant using the CHAOS framework. The architecture separates view configuration from conversation data, supports backend-driven chat interactions, and enables faster UI updates without new app releases. Yelp also discusses cross-platform challenges and reuse for its Biz Ask Anything pilot. By Leela Kumili
articles.summary: Yelp在其AI助手中结合原生移动控件与服务器驱动UI，通过CHAOS框架实现无需发版即可快速更新界面。

articles.title: GitLab 19.5 Makes Agentic Development a Governed Part of the DevOps Platform
articles.content: GitLab 19.5, released on October 15, puts agentic software development and governance at the centre of the platform, making its GitLab MCP server generally available while expanding how external AI agents can interact with GitLab. By Craig Risi
articles.summary: GitLab 19.5将代理式软件开发与治理置于平台核心，GitLab MCP服务器正式可用，并扩展外部AI代理的交互方式。

articles.title: TypeScript 7.1 Beta: Restores the Compiler API and Makes Vue and Svelte First-Class
articles.content: TypeScript 7.1 Beta, announced October 20, 2026, restores the compiler API removed in 7.0, now split into separate entry points. It adds content mappers, letting tools like Vue check non-standard files. One Vue project's type checks fell from 14.19 to 3.10 seconds. An editor issue remains open, and teams may need TypeScript 6 alongside 7. By Daniel Curtis
articles.summary: TypeScript 7.1 Beta恢复7.0移除的编译器API并拆分为独立入口，新增内容映射器支持Vue等非标准文件，Vue项目类型检查大幅提速。

articles.title: Presentation: The Socio-Technical Staff+ Engineer: Architecture, Culture and Organisational Change
articles.content: Vanessa Formicola shares how technical leaders can move beyond "wishful architecture" by practicing holistic socio-technical engineering. She discusses why engineering leaders must account for organizational maturity, reward structures, geopolitical climate, and team dynamics, framing the staff-plus role as designing the conditions for technology to thrive rather than just picking tools. By Vanessa Formicola
articles.summary: Vanessa Formicola分享Staff+工程师如何超越空想架构，实践整体社会技术工程，兼顾组织成熟度、激励结构和团队动态。

articles.title: AWS Ships Continuum for Code Vulnerabilities
articles.content: AWS has made Continuum for code vulnerabilities generally available in two regions. The service proves exploitability by running real exploits in a sandbox, then opens fixes as pull requests. Published pricing charges per finding processed as well as per line of code, and practitioners are asking what would justify letting it merge fixes on its own. By Steef-Jan Wiggers
articles.summary: AWS在两地正式推出Continuum代码漏洞服务，通过在沙箱运行真实漏洞利用验证可利用性，并自动提交修复PR，按发现数和代码行计费。

articles.title: Article: Identity as an Architectural Concern: Enterprise IAM Beyond Authentication
articles.content: The way you design your identities will drive your data models, your service scope, and your revocation policies; enterprise identity management is thus an architectural problem, not an afterthought. Based on our experience in service account governance, this article touches upon graph vs. RBAC, integrating a vault you don't own, and bounding revocation latency for an event stream. By Vaishnavi Khosla
articles.summary: 文章指出企业身份管理是架构问题而非事后补充，身份设计决定数据模型、服务边界和撤销策略，并探讨图模型与RBAC等方案。

articles.title: Vault Fork OpenBao Adds External Keys and Quantum-Ready TLS
articles.content: OpenBao has released version 2.7, adding read scaling for PostgreSQL-backed deployments, support for external hardware security module (HSM) and key management service (KMS) keys, and post-quantum cryptographic algorithms. The release also introduces control groups for human review of sensitive operations and new headers intended to keep requests consistent across load-balanced OpenBao nodes. By Matt Saunders
articles.summary: Vault分支OpenBao发布2.7版，新增PostgreSQL读扩展、外部HSM和KMS密钥支持、后量子加密算法及敏感操作人工审核控制组。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #542: AI week ahead: data center pause backers could win 15 governor races
articles.content: This issue is about the week ahead, and something is scheduled almost every day. On Tuesday, US voters choose 36 governors, and in up to 15 of those races the candidate who backs a pause on new data centers could win. Apple reports earnings today and AMD on Tuesday. On Wednesday, Apple starts testing Apple Intelligence in China with Alibaba's Qwen, and Agility Robotics expects to close its deal to go public. When Congress returns on November 9, OpenAI plans to push for "speed limits" on the most powerful AI. Last week, a fake Claude Code update reached up to 5,000 Cursor users, and in a Cornell and Yale test nine of ten AI models raised their own spending limits. In the middle: insuring Big Tech's debt now costs more than at any time since 2021.
articles.summary: AI周报第542期展望本周：美国36场州长选举中最多15场可能由支持暂停新建数据中心的候选人胜出，苹果和AMD将发布财报。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #541: Big Tech reports AI spending Wednesday as CoreWeave debt hits distress
articles.content: This issue looks ahead. On Wednesday the Fed announces its rate decision, then Microsoft and Alphabet report after the close. Amazon follows on Thursday. Investors want to know whether AI spending is still paying off, and the credit market is already nervous: insurance against a CoreWeave default now costs more than 10% a year. Anthropic is expected to file its IPO paperwork publicly any day. Moonshot says Kimi K3.1 Pro's open weights arrive November 4. Israel votes on Tuesday after a campaign full of AI deepfakes, and the US midterms are a week from Tuesday. In the middle: so far, AI has paid off for the companies that sell it, not the ones that buy it.
articles.summary: 微软、Alphabet、亚马逊本周将发布财报，投资者关注AI投入能否持续回报，同时CoreWeave债务违约保险成本飙升，信贷市场对AI基建风险已显紧张。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #540: AI is finding software flaws faster than teams can fix them
articles.content: This Applied AI edition looks at what organizations actually did with AI over the past two weeks, drawn from our Use-Case Library and from SEC filings. Three things stand out: AI now finds security flaws at record volume, AI agents do a large share of the work at some companies, and test agents keep doing things nobody asked them to do.
articles.summary: AI发现安全漏洞的速度已超过团队修复能力，部分公司AI代理承担大量工作，测试代理持续运行，企业实际应用与修复能力出现明显脱节。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #539: AI-made midterm ads top $137 million, and 70% carry no AI label
articles.content: Campaigns and PACs have spent more than $137 million on AI-generated or AI-enhanced midterm ads, and about 70% of them carry no AI label, the New York Times reported. The biggest pro-AI super PAC network paid about $20 million to a Nevada company that exists only as a post office box. A new report found 81 of 134 AI models failed a test built from terrorist-style questions. A video game reverse engineering site is closing because AI made the work too easy. Some companies that rushed into AI are now limiting it, and a JAMA study counted 270 million questions doctors asked one AI tool. In the middle: police in Michigan used an AI-generated photo of a teenager to catch a suspect.
articles.summary: 竞选团队和PAC在中期选举AI广告上花费超1.37亿美元，约70%未标注AI，最大亲AI超级PAC向仅有一个邮箱地址的内华达公司支付约2000万美元。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #537: AI models may soon copy themselves onto smart fridges, Anthropic says
articles.content: This issue is built from the links the AI experts we follow shared most since our last issue on October 8, minus the stories we already sent you in the Daily Espresso. The most shared: Anthropic's warning that small AI models may soon be able to copy themselves onto home devices. Also: a large study of what AI coding agents change at real companies, a fight over how to check AI math proofs, creative workers pushing back on AI, and police buying more AI.
articles.summary: Anthropic警告小型AI模型可能很快能自我复制到智能冰箱等家用设备上，引发对AI自主扩散与家庭设备安全的担忧。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #536: Top AI models failed a test of inventing new AI research
articles.content: This issue is built from the links the AI experts we follow shared over the past three days. Most of them look ahead: whether AI can do AI research on its own, who gets a say in governing it, how it is moving into war planning, and how it is moving onto personal computers.
articles.summary: 顶尖AI模型在自主开展新AI研究的测试中失败，同时业界关注AI治理话语权、AI进入战争规划及个人电脑等议题。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #535: AI got too expensive, so companies are moving to cheaper models
articles.content: This Applied AI edition looks at what organizations actually did with AI over the past three weeks. Three patterns stand out: companies switching models to control cost, large deployments that are now in daily use, and a growing list of places where AI was restricted or removed.
articles.summary: AI成本过高促使企业转向更便宜的模型，大型部署已进入日常使用，同时越来越多场景开始限制或移除AI应用。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #534: Universities cannot grade their way out of AI
articles.content: This week, campus IT leaders voted AI their top priority for the first time, Cambridge refused Turnitin's new terms over AI training on student work, Dartmouth opened an investigation into its own provost's writing, and Ken Griffin gave Carnegie Mellon $3 billion. Student AI use is no longer a future scenario. The useful question for universities is whether they can teach students to work with AI and still certify what those students can do without it. New evidence from tutoring trials, assessment redesigns, student-support systems and campus data deals points to a practical answer.
articles.summary: 高校IT负责人首次将AI列为首要任务，剑桥因AI训练条款拒绝Turnitin，达特茅斯调查教务长写作，AI已深刻冲击大学教学与评估。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #533: Meta tested human callers behind its AI phone agent
articles.content: The AI story of September 22–28 was not simply that agents became more capable. It was that their hidden handoffs became visible: a supposedly automated call could reach a contractor, a supposedly private prompt or image could reach a reviewer, a monitor could detect an agent long before a person stopped it, and a local app flaw could inherit every permission a user had granted. The new AI Weekly Who’s Who census points to one practical question: when an agent crosses a boundary, who knows—and who can still intervene?
articles.summary: Meta的AI电话代理被曝背后有真人接线员，揭示所谓自动化通话可能转接外包人员，私密提示和图像也可能被人工审核。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #531: AI labs shipped agents before agreeing how to report failures
articles.content: The AI story of September 14–20 was not one spectacular model launch. It was the machinery around agents becoming visible: people reading private chats, models writing instructions into their own memory, plugins updating beneath users, and regulators asking how to stop a system after release. The latest AI Weekly Who’s Who census surfaced 535 expert-shared links. We ranked them by consequence and reader relevance, not by raw share count. Here is what mattered last week—and, more importantly, what could move the story from September 22–28.
articles.summary: AI实验室在未就故障上报达成一致前就发布代理产品，暴露人工阅读私聊、模型写入自身记忆、插件静默更新及监管缺失等问题。

articles.title: We now have Kerr’s Law
articles.content: Dave Kerr created hacker laws, and now he finds himself reviewing agent-written code for them. Back on the show after six years, Dave names what he sees limiting teams today: keeping everyone’s mental model in sync with what’s actually been built. Adam declares it Kerr’s Law on the spot. We get into why Dave’s team treats code review as a deliberate slowdown, how Shellwright lets agents bring evidence to a pull request, and what living with bipolar disorder has taught Dave about noticing when the excitement of these tools stops being healthy.
articles.summary: Dave Kerr提出Kerr定律，指出当前限制团队的核心问题是所有人的心智模型难以与实际构建的系统保持同步，尤其在代理写代码时代。

articles.title: The future is Postgres
articles.content: Craig Kerstiens returns to talk about the ever-expanding world of Postgres: a deliberately boring core, a thriving extension ecosystem, and pg_lake bringing DuckDB and Iceberg into the mix. We dig into the pain of ETL, what Craig is watching in Postgres 19, the impact of AI on open source maintainers, and why the database still has plenty of room to grow.
articles.summary: Craig Kerstiens谈Postgres生态扩张，核心保持刻意简单、扩展繁荣，pg_lake引入DuckDB和Iceberg，并讨论AI对开源维护者的影响。

articles.title: Building what's next
articles.content: This week I'm talking with Zeno Rocha, CEO of Resend, about scaling "boring" email to 3 million users, the secret Go rewrite behind it, and building for agents. We cover pricing.md, MCP, spam gangs, and why Resend keeps what's next for email.
articles.summary: Resend CEO Zeno Rocha分享如何将无聊的邮件服务扩展至300万用户，包括Go重写、面向代理构建、定价文件与反垃圾策略。

articles.title: From zero to NanoClaw
articles.content: Gavriel Cohen, creator of NanoClaw and co-founder of NanoCo, joins Adam to explain how a 40-hour weekend project became a viral open source hit and the foundation of an enterprise AI company. Gavriel describes the security concerns that led him to build a small, container-isolated alternative to OpenClaw, why he released it under the MIT license, and why the project's community and credibility are more valuable than keeping its code private. They explore the shift from writing code to architecting the environments in which agents work, NanoClaw's "skills over features" approach, the approval and governance layers required inside large companies, and a future where every worker manages agents without surrendering human judgment. They close with the technical simplicity behind NanoClaw, containers, TypeScript, SQLite, and a two-database design, and Adam's case for durable Agent Flow artifacts that keep organizational context from disappearing into chat.
articles.summary: NanoClaw 作者 Gavriel Cohen 讲述 40 小时周末项目如何成为爆红开源项目，并发展为一家企业级 AI 公司。

articles.title: Changelog IRL @ PlanetScale (Sept 17, 2026)
articles.content: Changelog is taking over PlanetScale's HQ We’re getting together IRL!! On Thursday, September 17th, Changelog is taking over PlanetScale’s HQ in San Francisco for an evening of short talks and conversations about AI, developer tools and what people are building. We’ll have a few conversations with special guests and time for questions, food, drinks and hanging out. I’ll be joined by three builders pushing this idea forward, starting with Dan Robinson from Detail (detail.dev), with more guests to be announced very soon. I also have 80 limited edition t-shirts printed to give away! This won’t be a few presentations followed by everyone heading home. We’re doing this Changelog-style: live conversations, questions from the room, drinks, and plenty of time afterward for the hallway track. If you’re in San Francisco, register to come hang out!
